doc.title: Howie Shear interviewed by Monk Rowe, Dunkirk, New York, October 11, 2014

title: Writing Jazz Improvisation Simplified
summary: He wrote his book to simplify jazz teaching, which he found too academic, like calculus without arithmetic.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well I’m interested in — there’s a description here about how you define some of jazz teaching as like higher math. Higher mathematics. And that really rang a bell with me because I have felt the same thing and I’m wondering if you can sort of sum up your thoughts.
No. Well you were — about the book and method you put out.
And it was an attempt to simplify.

Simplify jazz, yeah. Jazz Improvisation Simplified. Yeah when I was first learning how to play I would go to certain people in the area where I was going to school, before I started school, before I started my master’s in jazz studies. And they couldn’t seem to explain it to me. That’s a lot of the old-timers — at that time they were old-timers. They sort of learned how to play with records. They didn’t have books or academics on how to play jazz. And they didn’t explain it very well. So I said I’d better figure it out. And then I looked at some books in the stores (when they had music stores) and the books were very difficult to understand and I felt like I was going to school to learn quantum physics, in which case I go oh let me figure this out myself. So I sort of figured it out myself. And

then over the years I said I should write a book for my students particularly, and anybody else that wanted it obviously, but to explain all the books that were at a very high level. There were no books that led up to that. And so it’s like learning calculus without learning the essence of arithmetic and the foundations of arithmetic. So I wrote this book and I tried to simplify everything that you would get. But yet it’s not a dumbed-down version, but it’s what players need to know to improvise quite well actually. So it’s not simplified for just like the novice or the grade school kid. It’s really like Charlie Parker played jazz and after him. But a lot of people who wrote these books are very — at a high level and they just like to flex their bebop muscles, and they like to speak in a very high academic language to make them appear smarter than they really are, although a lot of them are very smart people, don’t get me wrong. But they didn’t really think about the person that didn’t really know how to play. They thought about the person that already knew how to play. And I wanted to think about the person that didn’t really know how to get started. And I get a lot of emails today thanking me for writing that particular book. And I’m glad about that. Because I think it’s important. Because we want to continue the art form.
